Content:
The equation of the normal line to the curve [MATH: y = f(x)] at the point [MATH: P(x_1,y_1),] in point-slope form, is given by
[MATH: y - y_1 = m (x - x_1), \hspace{1cm} m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}.]
Here, [MATH: m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}] because the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line, and [MATH: f'(x_1)] represents the slope of the tangent line to [MATH: y=f(x)] at the point [MATH: (x_1,y_1).]

Content:
For example, suppose we want to compute the equation of the normal line to the curve [MATH: y=x^2] at the point [MATH: A(1,1).] This normal line is the dashed line shown below, which is perpendicular to the solid tangent line.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/424a5b155291a888240f9e553dc0c7be]

Content:
Since [MATH: y=x^2,] we have [MATH: f(x)=x^2.] We begin by calculating the derivative of [MATH: f(x)\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: f'(x) = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(x^2)= 2x]

Content:
At [MATH: A(1,1),] the slope of the tangent line is given by
[MATH: f'(1) = 2(1) = 2.]

Content:
However, we want the normal line, and the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:
[MATH: m = -\dfrac{1}{f'(1)} = -\dfrac{1}{2}]

Content:
Finally, we work out the equation of the normal line using the point-slope form:

Content:
[MATH: y − 1|= − (1)/(2)(x − 1); y|= − (x)/(2) + (1)/(2) + 1; y|= − (x)/(2) + (3)/(2).]

Content:
Therefore, the equation of the normal line is [MATH: y=-\dfrac x 2 + \dfrac 3 2.] We could also write this in standard form as [MATH: x+2y=3.]

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: f(x)=x^3 - x^2.] First, we compute the derivative: [MATH: f^{′}(x) = (d)/(dx)(x^{3} − x^{2}) = 3x^{2} − 2x]

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point [MATH: (1, 0){:}] [MATH: m = f^{′}(1) = 3 − 2 = 1]

Therefore, the slope of the normal line [MATH: m'] is [MATH: m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=-1.]

Finally, the equation of the normal line is [MATH: y − 0|= − (x − 1); y|= − x + 1.]

Therefore, [MATH: p=-1] and [MATH: q=1.]

sections.normalized_html:
Taking the derivative, we have [MATH: f^{′}(x)|= (d)/(dx)(2sqrt(x) − 4x); = (d)/(dx)(2x^{1/2} − 4x); = x^{− 1/2} − 4.]

So the slope of the tangent line is [MATH: m=f'(1) = (1)^{-1/2} - 4 = -3,] and therefore the slope of the normal line is [MATH: m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = \dfrac 1 3.]

The equation of the normal line is [MATH: y − (− 2)|= (1)/(3)(x − 1); y + 2|= (1)/(3)(x − 1); y|= (1)/(3)x − (1)/(3) − 2; y|= (1)/(3)x − (7)/(3).]

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the [MATH: x]-axis by setting [MATH: y=0] and solving the resulting equation. We get [MATH: (1)/(3)x − (7)/(3)|= 0; (1)/(3)x|= (7)/(3); x|= 7.]

Therefore, the normal line intersects the [MATH: x]-axis at [MATH: (7,0).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The equation of the normal line to the curve [MATH: y = f(x)] at the point [MATH: P(x_1,y_1),] in point-slope form, is given by
[MATH: y - y_1 = m (x - x_1), \hspace{1cm} m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}.]
Here, [MATH: m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}] because the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line, and [MATH: f'(x_1)] represents the slope of the tangent line to [MATH: y=f(x)] at the point [MATH: (x_1,y_1).]

Content:
For example, suppose we want to compute the equation of the normal line to the curve [MATH: y=x^2] at the point [MATH: A(1,1).] This normal line is the dashed line shown below, which is perpendicular to the solid tangent line.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/424a5b155291a888240f9e553dc0c7be]

Content:
Since [MATH: y=x^2,] we have [MATH: f(x)=x^2.] We begin by calculating the derivative of [MATH: f(x)\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: f'(x) = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(x^2)= 2x]

Content:
At [MATH: A(1,1),] the slope of the tangent line is given by
[MATH: f'(1) = 2(1) = 2.]

Content:
However, we want the normal line, and the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:
[MATH: m = -\dfrac{1}{f'(1)} = -\dfrac{1}{2}]

Content:
Finally, we work out the equation of the normal line using the point-slope form:

Content:
[MATH: y − 1|= − (1)/(2)(x − 1); y|= − (x)/(2) + (1)/(2) + 1; y|= − (x)/(2) + (3)/(2).]

Content:
Therefore, the equation of the normal line is [MATH: y=-\dfrac x 2 + \dfrac 3 2.] We could also write this in standard form as [MATH: x+2y=3.]

---
